title: If You’re Trying To Do This Fast, You’re Doing It Wrong
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday argues that speed reading is not only a scam but a misunderstanding of why we read at all. He contrasts the culture of 2x audiobooks, word-flashing apps, and book-count bragging with great readers such as Didion, Emerson, Montaigne, John Adams, Patton, and Octavia Butler, who read slowly, actively, and deliberately, filling commonplace books and margins. His central claim is that people who read a lot simply spend a lot of time reading, a point he supports with Tyler Cowen and the Zen story of the student Banzo, told that hurry would only lengthen his apprenticeship. Holiday then describes treating reading as a professional obligation that makes him a better parent, husband, and boss. The essay closes with a plug for his Read to Lead course, but its substance is a defense of patient, attentive reading as the only path to real wisdom.
points: Holiday observes that across great readers past and present he cannot find one who credited their volume of reading to reading fast.
The Banzo story makes the point that a student in a hurry learns the slowest.
He argues that the difficulty of reading is the point, since the payoff of a good book takes time to extract.
Holiday reframes reading as his actual job, an investment that improves him as a parent, spouse, and leader.
quotes: I get this a lot. Because I talk about reading quite a bit, people assume I am a speed reader. I'm not.
Here we are with people hung up on how many books they read instead of how much they get out of the books they read.
Great readers take their time. Great readers read deliberately. Great readers read actively.
People who read a lot of books spend a lot of time reading. There's no way around this.
In that case," the master said, "it shall take seventy years. A student in a hurry learns the slowest.
The whole point of reading is that it's hard, but that the hard is worth it. The whole point of a book is that there is a lot in there and it will take time to get it out.
It makes me a better person. It makes me a better parent. It makes me a better husband. It makes me a better boss. It makes me better at everything I do. So I take it seriously. I invest in it.
